iroquois_hino.name: Hurl the thunderbolts and lightning of the storm
iroquois_hino.notes: As leader of the winged race of Thunderers (the Hadu'i / Hinon brothers), He-no travels the western clouds carrying a pouch of thunderbolts and a basket of chert boulders which he casts at evil spirits; the bolts that miss fall to earth as lightning.

sources.reference: Harriet Maxwell Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908)

iroquois_hino.name: Slay the great horned water-serpents
iroquois_hino.notes: He-no is the sworn enemy of the monstrous horned serpent (Oniare) that lurks in lakes and rivers; he tracks and destroys these and other monsters with his bolts, keeping the ordered world safe for the people.

sources.reference: Erminnie A. Smith, Myths of the Iroquois (BAE 2nd Annual Report, 1883)

iroquois_hino.name: Bring the life-giving rains that ripen the crops
iroquois_hino.notes: Revered as the bringer of the rains that nourish the corn, beans and squash; addressed in the Thanksgiving Address among the powers that sustain the people.

sources.reference: Smith, Myths of the Iroquois (1883)

iroquois_teharonhiawako.name: Make the gentle rivers, food plants and useful animals
iroquois_teharonhiawako.notes: The Sapling/good twin forms straight rivers, fruit-bearing plants and docile creatures such as the deer, in contrast to his brother Flint who makes rapids, thorns and predators; he gives humankind the arts of living and the ceremonies.

sources.reference: J. N. B. Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology, First Part (BAE 21st Annual Report, 1903)

iroquois_teharonhiawako.name: Overcome the destructive twin in the world-shaping contest
iroquois_teharonhiawako.notes: In the final duel that fixes the order of the world Sapling defeats Flint (in most recensions with deer-horn as the lethal weapon), securing day, summer and life for the people and confining his brother to the cold half of the year.

sources.reference: Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology (1903)

iroquois_tawiskaron.name: Make the hardships of the world — rapids, frost, thorns and monsters
iroquois_tawiskaron.notes: The flinty Evil-Minded twin answers his brother's good creation by spoiling it: he raises rapids and waterfalls, brings frost and winter, makes predatory beasts and the monstrous serpents, and is overcome in the final contest.

sources.reference: J. N. B. Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology, First Part (BAE 21st Annual Report, 1903)

iroquois_tekawerahkwa.name: Conceive the rival Twins by the Wind and die bearing them
iroquois_tekawerahkwa.notes: Impregnated by the West Wind, she dies when the destructive twin Flint forces his way out through her side; her death is the origin of the Twins who shape the world.

sources.reference: J. N. B. Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology, First Part (BAE 21st Annual Report, 1903)

iroquois_tekawerahkwa.name: Give the staple crops from her buried body
iroquois_tekawerahkwa.notes: From her grave grow the Three Sisters — maize from her breast, beans and squash from her hands and navel — together with tobacco from her head; she is the source of the people's food.

sources.reference: Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology (1903)

itelmen_sinanevt.name: Prevail by cleverness and craft in the folktales
itelmen_sinanevt.notes: Daughter of the raven-creator Kutkh and Miti and one of the most frequent protagonists of recorded Itelmen tales, where she succeeds through industry and wit against ogres and against her foolish kin.

sources.reference: Waldemar Jochelson / Jesup North Pacific Expedition, Kamchadal (Itelmen) folklore

itelmen_miti.name: Help create the world and mother the first family
itelmen_miti.notes: With her husband the raven-creator Kutkh, Miti is said to help fashion the world and bears their children — sons Ememqut and Kotxanamtalxan and daughters including Sinanevt — the Kamchatkan first family.

sources.reference: S. P. Krasheninnikov, Account of the Land of Kamchatka (1755)

japanese_sanetomo.name: Compose waka of the first rank in the archaic Manyo manner
japanese_sanetomo.notes: Tutored at a distance by Fujiwara no Teika, the third Kamakura shogun left some 700 poems collected in the Kinkai Wakashu and a verse in the Ogura Hyakunin Isshu, prized for a vigorous archaic style.

sources.reference: Minamoto no Sanetomo, Kinkai Wakashu

iroquois_hino.name: Thunder invocation and thanksgiving
iroquois_hino.cadence: at thunderstorms and in the seasonal thanksgiving cycle
iroquois_hino.notes: The Thunderer is invoked during thunderstorms and named with gratitude in the Thanksgiving Address (Ohenton Karihwatehkwen) among the powers that bring rain and protect the people; tobacco is burned to him.

sources.reference: Erminnie A. Smith, Myths of the Iroquois (BAE 2nd Annual Report, 1883)

japanese_amaterasu.name: Worship at the Ise Grand Shrine (Naiku)
japanese_amaterasu.cadence: perpetual; Shikinen Sengu rebuilding every 20 years
japanese_amaterasu.notes: Amaterasu is enshrined at the Inner Shrine (Naiku) of Ise, where the Yata-no-Kagami mirror is kept as her sacred body; the Shikinen Sengu reconstruction of the shrine has been performed roughly every twenty years since 690 CE.

sources.reference: Ise Jingu tradition; Engishiki (10th c.)

japanese_susanoo.name: Gion Matsuri
japanese_susanoo.notes: Centred on Yasaka (Gion) Shrine in Kyoto, the festival originates in the goryo-e of 869 CE to placate the pestilence-deity (Susanoo / Gozu Tenno) during an epidemic; its yamaboko floats process to purify the city and ward off plague.

sources.reference: Yasaka Jinja tradition; Gion goryo-e of 869

japanese_inari.name: Worship at Fushimi Inari Taisha
japanese_inari.cadence: perpetual; hatsu-uma rite in early spring
japanese_inari.notes: Head of tens of thousands of Inari shrines, founded by the Hata clan in 711 CE; worshippers pass through corridors of vermilion torii and present offerings of rice, sake and fried tofu (aburaage / inari-zushi) to the fox-messengers.

sources.reference: Fushimi Inari Taisha tradition; Karen A. Smyers, The Fox and the Jewel (1999)

japanese_hachiman.name: Hojo-e (rite of releasing living beings)
japanese_hachiman.notes: The Iwashimizu Hojo-e, established 863 CE (and the Hakozaki/Usa observances), expresses Hachiman's Buddhist character: fish and birds are released into river and sea as an act of merit and prayer for peace.

sources.reference: Iwashimizu Hachimangu / Usa Jingu tradition

japanese_konohanasakuya_hime.name: Worship at Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha
japanese_konohanasakuya_hime.notes: Head of some 1,300 Asama/Sengen shrines, where Mount Fuji itself is revered as her divine body; she is invoked for safe childbirth, against fire, and as patroness of sake-brewing.

sources.reference: Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha tradition

japanese_okuninushi.name: Worship at Izumo Taisha
japanese_okuninushi.cadence: perpetual; Kamiari-sai in the tenth lunar month
japanese_okuninushi.notes: The great shrine promised to Okuninushi at the land-cession (kuni-yuzuri); at Kamiari-zuki the kami of Japan are believed to gather there, and he is petitioned as the god of en-musubi (binding of marriages and bonds).

sources.reference: Kojiki, Book 1 (kuni-yuzuri); Izumo Taisha tradition

japanese_omononushi.name: Worship at Omiwa Shrine (Mount Miwa)
japanese_omononushi.notes: One of Japan's oldest shrines: it has no honden, for Mount Miwa itself is the deity's body, fronted by a triple torii before the forbidden mountain. Offerings of sake and eggs are made to the snake-god, and a cedar-ball (sugidama) marks his patronage of sake-brewing.

sources.reference: Nihon Shoki, Sujin chapter; Omiwa Jinja tradition

japanese_kagutsuchi.name: Ho-shizume-no-matsuri (fire-pacification rite)
japanese_kagutsuchi.notes: Worshipped as Homusubi at Atago and Akiba shrines as the god of fire and the forge; the court held the Ho-shizume rite twice a year to placate him and avert palace conflagrations.

sources.reference: Engishiki, Norito (Ho-shizume-no-matsuri); Atago/Akiba shrine tradition

japanese_tametomo.name: Apotropaic veneration as a smallpox-queller
japanese_tametomo.cadence: during epidemics; protective charms for children
japanese_tametomo.notes: From the legend that no smallpox struck Hachijo-jima because the exiled Tametomo had driven off the smallpox demon, his image was made into hoso-e (smallpox pictures) and papier-mache charms given to sick children to ward off the disease.

sources.reference: Edo-period hoso-e (smallpox-print) tradition

attributes.name: A winged man (sometimes a giant bird)
attributes.notes: Depicted as a winged man, leader of the Thunderers, who may shift between human and great-bird form; dwells in the clouds of the far west.

sources.reference: Harriet Maxwell Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908)
Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908)

attributes.name: Solar radiance; the sun emerging from the Rock-Cave
attributes.notes: Imaged as the light of the sun, most famously at her emergence from the Ama-no-Iwato (Heavenly Rock-Cave); her body is held to reside in the Yata-no-Kagami mirror at Ise.

sources.reference: Kojiki, Book 1 (Rock-Cave episode)

sacredAnimals.name: Rooster (the long-crowing cocks that called her forth)

sources.reference: Kojiki, Book 1 (the 'long-singing birds' before the Rock-Cave)

attributes.name: Vermilion torii and red votive bibs
attributes.notes: Inari shrines are marked by ranks of vermilion (red) torii and by fox statues dressed in red yodarekake bibs; the colour red is itself emblematic of Inari.

sources.reference: Fushimi Inari Taisha tradition

attributes.name: Sheaf of rice / the fox bearing a key or jewel
attributes.notes: Associated with the rice-sheaf and with fox imagery in which the messenger-fox holds a key (to the granary) or a wish-fulfilling jewel.

sources.reference: Karen A. Smyers, The Fox and the Jewel (1999)

sacredAnimals.name: White fox (byakko / myobu), the messenger of Inari

sources.reference: Fushimi Inari Taisha tradition

sacredPlants.name: Rice (ine), the staple under Inari's protection

sources.reference: Inari shrine tradition

sacredAnimals.name: Yamata-no-Orochi, the eight-forked serpent he slew

sources.reference: Kojiki, Book 1 (slaying of Yamata-no-Orochi)

sacredPlants.name: Chimaki rush-bundles (su-shimenawa amulets of Gion)
sacredPlants.notes: The Gion chimaki — bundles of rushes hung at doorways — derive from the tradition of Somin Shorai protected from pestilence by Susanoo / Gozu Tenno.

sources.reference: Yasaka Jinja / Somin Shorai tradition

attributes.name: The bow-and-arrow of the warrior-god on Genji banners
attributes.notes: Tutelary kami of the Minamoto (Genji); his emblem is the bow and arrow, and his name appears on samurai war-banners.

sources.reference: Minamoto (Genji) warrior-cult tradition

sacredAnimals.name: Dove / pigeon (hato), the messenger of Hachiman

sources.reference: Iwashimizu Hachimangu tradition (white doves)

attributes.name: Seated goddess playing the biwa lute
attributes.notes: Most commonly imaged as a beautiful goddess holding and playing the biwa, after the Indian Saraswati with her vina; in the Uga-Benzaiten form a human-headed white snake (Ugajin) coils above her head.

sources.reference: Japanese Buddhist iconography of Benzaiten / Uga-Benzaiten

sacredAnimals.name: White snake (her messenger and emblem of wealth)

sources.reference: Benzaiten / Ugajin tradition

attributes.name: Smiling, seated god with fishing-rod and a red sea-bream
attributes.notes: Shown laughing or smiling, seated (he still has difficulty standing), holding a fishing-rod in the right hand and a large red sea-bream (tai) under the left arm, wearing a tall pointed kazaori-eboshi cap.

sources.reference: Shichifukujin iconography; Nishinomiya Jinja tradition

sacredAnimals.name: Red sea-bream (tai), the auspicious fish he holds

sources.reference: Ebisu iconography

attributes.name: Green-skinned oni-like demon bearing a great wind-bag
attributes.notes: Depicted as a fearsome, often green-skinned wind-demon running across the sky with the kazabukuro (wind-sack) stretched across his shoulders, from which he looses the winds; canonically paired with Raijin, as in the Sanjusangendo statues and Tawaraya Sotatsu's screen.

sources.reference: Sanjusangendo Kamakura-period statues; Tawaraya Sotatsu, Wind God and Thunder God screen

attributes.name: Red-skinned oni-like demon ringed by thunder-drums
attributes.notes: Imaged as a muscular, often red-skinned demon encircled by a ring of taiko drums which he beats with hammers (bachi) to make thunder; canonically paired with Fujin in the Sanjusangendo statuary and the Sotatsu screen.

sources.reference: Sanjusangendo Kamakura-period statues; Tawaraya Sotatsu, Wind God and Thunder God screen

attributes.name: Great dragon dwelling in the coral undersea palace
attributes.notes: Imaged as a vast dragon (or a dragon-bodied king) holding the tide-ruling jewels in his undersea palace Ryugu-jo, built of coral and crystal; his daughters are Toyotama-hime and Tamayori-hime.

sources.reference: Kojiki, Book 1 (Watatsumi's palace; the tide-jewels)

sacredAnimals.name: Wani (sea-monster/crocodile-dragon) and the turtle, his messengers

sources.reference: Kojiki, Book 1 (the wani that bears Hoori home)

sacredAnimals.name: The White Hare of Inaba, whom he healed

sources.reference: Kojiki, Book 1 (the Hare of Inaba)

attributes.name: The sacred cedar of Miwa (cedar-ball / sugidama)
attributes.notes: His patronage of sake-brewing is marked by the sugidama, a ball of cedar boughs hung at breweries; the cedar is the sacred tree of Mount Miwa.

sources.reference: Omiwa Jinja tradition

sacredAnimals.name: White snake, the form of the Miwa deity

sources.reference: Kojiki, Book 1 (the serpent-form revealed by the thread)

sacredPlants.name: Cedar (sugi), the sacred tree of Mount Miwa

sources.reference: Omiwa Jinja tradition

sacredPlants.name: Cherry blossom (sakura), her emblem and namesake
sacredPlants.notes: Her name means roughly 'tree-blossom blooming princess'; the fleeting cherry blossom is her sign and a symbol of transient beauty.

sources.reference: Sengen/Asama shrine tradition; Konohanasakuya-hime mythology

attributes.name: The Ten Sacred Treasures (tokusa-no-kandakara)
attributes.notes: Bestowed on him by the heavenly kami when he descended in the Rock-Boat: two mirrors, one sword, four magatama beads and three scarves (hire), used in the soul-pacifying mitama-furi rite and kept at Isonokami Shrine.

sources.reference: Sendai Kuji Hongi, Tenson Hongi; Isonokami Jingu tradition
